full_judgment:
2. The pre-emptor-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 3 of 1996, previously numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 87 of 1990 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet for pre-emption of the case land measuring 0.12 acre under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. The case of the pre-emptor is that Israil Miah, one of the recorded tenants of case plot No. 597 transferred a portion of his share to Haji Abdul Gafur, Syed Arjumand Ali, Mafajjal Hossain and Mahmud Hossain by a registered deed of sale dated 4-4-1965. Abdul Gafur sold a portion of land from his share to one Golam Rahmani Khan by a registered deed of sale dated 18-12-1975 who died leaving behind the pre-emptors and his heirs and thus the pre-emptors became co-sharers in the case holding. Syed Arjumand Ali transferred 0.30 acre of land out of his share to his daughter-in-law by a registered deed in lieu of her dower and subsequently Syed Arjumand Ali and his daughter-in-law by a registered sale deed sold 0.36 acre of land to Mainuddin and Rawshan Ara Begum who are the opposite party Nos. 3 and 4 respectively in the pre-emption. The Government also acquied a part of the land purchased by Mainuddin and Rawshan Ara Begum for Shahjalal Upashahar project. The pre-emptor subsequently came to know that opposite party Nos. 3 and 4 in the pre-emption case have transferred the case land to pre-emptee opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 and thereafter the pre-emptors obtained certified copy of the sale deed dated 23-7-1990 and 7-10-1990 and got the definite knowledge of the impugned transfer although they were not served with any notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the preemptees are strangers to the case holding and thus the pre-emptors were compelled to file the present case. 

 4. The present petitioner and another resisted the pre-emption by filing a joint written objection denying the allegations made in the pre-emption petition. Their case is that opposite parities Nos. 3 and 4 of the pre-emption case after purchasing the case land by registered deed on 16-12-1975 created separate khatian No. 534/1 in respect of the case land on the basis of Mutation Case No. 1933 of 1983-84 and thereafter they sold their purchased .36 acres of land including the case land to the preemptees by registered deed 23-7-1990. The pre-emptees after purchase got the land mutated in their names in Mutation Case No. 1762 of 1990 and created separate Mutation Khatian No. 687. Preemptee-opposite party No. 2 sold his share of the case land to pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 (present petitioner) by a registered deed dated 6-9-1990 whereupon pre-emptee-opposite-party No. 1 got khatian No. 687 created in his sole name in Mutation Case No. 272 of 1991. On the other hand, the pre-emptors also created separate khatian No. 534/3 in respect of their .13 acre in Mutation Case No. 633 of 1984-85. Even then the pre-emptors were informed about the impugned transfer prior to the same, and in fact, pre-emptor No. 1 himself fixed the consideration money of the impugned transfer. Moreover, the pre-emptors and their two brothers had transferred their shares in the case holding by registered sale deeds dated 23-12-85, 17-5-1990, 15-2-1990 and 9-7-1990 and totally extinguished their interest in the case holding. The case land has been included within Sylhet Paurashava (now City Corporation) by Gazette notification dated 23-10-1990 and, as such, the instant pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act filed on 28-10-1990 is not maintainable. The case has been filed on false pleas with a view to grabbing the preemptee's land invoking wrong provision of law. The pre-emptee-petitioner has developed the case land spending Taka 10 lac and thus the case is liable to be dismissed with cost. The opposite parties Nos. 3 and 4(the vendors) also contes-ted the case by filing a separate written objection. 

 8. Mr Probir Neogi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the lower appellate Court passed the impugned judgment depending on mere surmises and conjecture and did not at all apply its judicial mind while disposing of the appeal and passed the impugned judgment which is not tenable in the eyes of law and, as such the said judgment is liable to be set aside. He also submits that the lower appellate Court failed to appreciate that the pre-emptors are not the co-sharers of the case holding. He points out that the trial Court took into consideration the fact that the khatian number of the pre-emptor is 534/3 which was exhibited before the trial Court as Exhibit A(1)(i) and the land under pre-emption purchased by the present petitioner is in khatian No. 534/1 as exhibited in Exhibit A(a)(ii) which has been admitted by PW 1 in his deposition and, on the basis of this fact, the pre-emption case was disallowed by the trial Court which has not been reversed by the lower appellate Court. He next submits that due to non-consideration of this material evidence on record and misreading the facts of the case, the appellate Court below has arrived at such a decision which cannot be sustained under law. The learned Lawyer points out that the case land was included in Sylhet Paurashava by a notification and thus the land was declared as an urban land and the present case filed subsequently under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which deals with pre-emption of cultivable land, is not maintainable. He submits that it is also evident from record that PW 1 stated in his deposition that he will establish a rod, cement shop in the suit land if the pre-emption case is allowed. The learned lawyer submits that since the case holdings are different, the pre-emptor cannot claim pre-emption as a co-sharer. In support of his contention the learned Lawyer has referred a decision as reported in 50 DLR (AD) 96. He also points out that as Exhibits A(1)(i) were already admitted into evidence and marked as exhibits without any objection, the question of inadmissibility of these documents cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time. In support of his contention the learned Lawyer has referred a decision as reported in 44 DLR (AD) 162. The learned Counsel then submits that the pre-emption law as far as possible should be followed strictly because it operates as a clog on a citizen's right to deal with his property in the way he likes. In support of his contention, the learned Lawyer has referred a decision as reported in 32 DLR (AD) 54. The learned Advocate lastly, submits that the judgment of the lower appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal as the lower appellate Court reversed the decision of trial Court without adverting to the material findings upon which the decision of the trial Court was founded. 

 12. On this vital point and the finding of the trial Court that the pre-emptors are not co-sharers, the lower appellate Court did not say anything while reversing the judgment of the trial Court. Since the khatians are different, the pre-emptor cannot be held to be a co-sharer in the case holding and, as such, they are not entitled to pre-emption. The emptors, it appears from the materials on record, have no locus standi to file the pre-emption case in respect of khatian No. 534/1 (Exhibit A(a)(ii). The trial Court also found that the case of pre-emption was filed on 28-10-1990 under section 96(1) of the Acquisition and Tenancy Act whereas the Gazette notification dated 23-10-1990 shows that the Government took over the case plot within the Sylhet Municipality and thus it became urban land for which claim cannot be made by the pre-emptors for pre-emption under the provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The lower appellate Court though found that the Gazette notification was published on 23-10-1990 and the case was filed on 28-10-1990 but observed that the transfer took place earlier on 23-7-1990. The lower appellate Court ought to have considered that the statutory provision providing the curtailment of the owner's right to deal with his property must be construed very strictly and this right of pre-emption must be allowed to a claimant in consideration of his necessity and not as a matter of luxury. It is evident from the materials on record that the land in question being non-agricultural in nature, which is an admitted fact, the application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable. The pre-emptor has no locus standi to file the case, as he is not the co-sharer on the case holding number of this non-agricultural land.
